cards.front: Can you write if (a) when a is an int?
cards.extra: Unlike C, there is no notion of non-zero being true. The book notes this restriction exists to catch mistakes at compile time.

cards.front: What is the one difference between while and do-while?
cards.extra: The condition is tested after the body. In a while, a false first test means the body never runs at all.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a for loop, and when do they run?
cards.back: Initialisation once; test before every iteration; step after every iteration
cards.extra: Any of the three may be empty, which is how an infinite for(;;) is written. The test is checked before the body, not after.

cards.front: A variable is declared in the for initialisation. What is its scope?
cards.back: The loop statement itself — it disappears after the loop
cards.extra: Declaring int i = 0 inside the for header keeps the counter out of the enclosing method, which is why two loops can reuse the same name.

cards.front: What is the difference between break and continue?
cards.back: break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next iteration
cards.extra: Both abandon the rest of the current pass. break exits entirely, continue re-tests the condition and goes round again.

cards.back: No — but it has labelled break and continue
cards.extra: A label before a loop lets an inner loop exit the outer one: outer: for(...) { ... break outer; }. It is the only jump Java kept.

cards.extra: It compares for equality against case labels and jumps. Unlike if-else it never evaluates a range or a boolean expression.
